On the parabolic-elliptic limit
of the doubly parabolic Keller–Segel system
modelling chemotaxis

Piotr Biler Affiliation:  Affiliation:  Instytut Matematyczny, Uniwersytet Wrocławski, pl. Grunwaldzki 2/4, 50–384 Wrocław, POLAND Email: Piotr.Biler@math.uni.wroc.pl    Lorenzo Brandolese Affiliation:  Affiliation:  Université de Lyon, Université Lyon 1,Institut Camille Jordan, CNRS UMR 5208,43 bd. du 11 Novembre, 69622 Villeurbanne Cedex, FRANCE Email: brandolese@math.univ-lyon1.fr
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We establish new convergence results, in strong topologies, for solutions of the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel system in the plane, to the corresponding solutions of the parabolic-elliptic model, as a physical parameter goes to zero. Our main tools are suitable space-time estimates, implying the global existence of slowly decaying (in general, nonintegrable) solutions for these models, under a natural smallness assumption.

Dedicated to the memory of Andrzej Hulanicki

1 Introduction

We consider two related nonlinear parabolic systems which are frequently used as models for a description of chemotactic phenomena, including the aggregation of microorganisms caused by a chemoattractant, i.e. a chemical whose concentration gradient governs the oriented movement of those microorganisms. The parabolic character of the systems comes from the diffusion described by the Laplacians. A version of the system (PE) below is also used in astrophysics as a model of the evolution of a cloud of self-gravitating particles in the mean field approximation.

The first one is the classical parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel system

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇φ),Δ​φ+u=0,u⁡(0)=u0.x∈ℝ2,t>0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla\varphi),\\ &\Delta\varphi+u=0,\\ &u(0)=u_{0}.\;\end{aligned}\right.\qquad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2},\ t>0, (PE)

Here, u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t), φ=φ⁡(x,t)\varphi=\varphi(x,t) are either functions or suitable (tempered) distributions. When u≥0u\geq 0, φ≥0\varphi\geq 0, they may be interpreted as concentrations (densities) of microorganisms and chemicals, respectively.

The second one is the parabolic-parabolic system

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇φ),τ​φt=Δ​φ+u,u(0)=u0,φ(0)=0,x∈ℝ2,t>0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla\varphi),\\ &\tau\varphi_{t}=\Delta\varphi+u,\\ &u(0)=u_{0},\ \ \varphi(0)=0,\end{aligned}\right.\qquad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2},\ t>0, (PP)

where τ>0\tau>0 is a fixed parameter. Each of the models can be considered as a single nonlinear parabolic equation for uu with a nonlocal (either in xx or in (x,t)(x,t)) nonlinearity since the term ∇φ\nabla\varphi can be expressed as a linear integral operator acting on uu. In the latter model, the variations of the concentration φ\varphi are governed by the linear nonhomogeneous heat equation, and therefore are slower than in the former system, where the response of φ\varphi to the variations of uu is instantaneous, and described by the integral operator (−Δ)−1(-\Delta)^{-1} whose kernel has a singularity. Thus, one may expect that the evolution described by (PE) might be faster than that for (PP), especially for large values of τ\tau when the diffusion of φ\varphi is rather slow compared to that of uu. Moreover, the nonlinear effects for (PE) should manifest themselves faster than for (PP).

The theory of the system (PE) is relatively well developed, in particular when this is studied in a bounded domain in ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, d=1, 2, 3d=1,\,2,\,3, with the homogeneous Neumann conditions for uu and φ\varphi at the boundary of the domain. One of the most intriguing properties of (PE) considered for positive and integrable solutions uu in d=2d=2 case is the existence of a threshold value 8​π8\pi of mass M≡∫u⁡(x,t)​𝑑xM\equiv\int u(x,t)\,{\rm d}x, see the pioneering work [17] and [1, 3]. Namely, if u0≥0u_{0}\geq 0 is such that ∫u0​(x)​𝑑x>8​π\int u_{0}(x)\,{\rm d}x>8\pi, then any regular, positive solution uu of (PE) cannot be global in time. We refer the reader for a fine description of the asymptotic behaviour of integrable solutions of (PE) in the subcritical case M<8​πM<8\pi to [11] and to [10] for the limit case M=8​πM=8\pi. See also [8, 9] in the radially symmetric case. The higher dimensional versions of (PE) have been also extensively studied, cf., e.g., [2, 6, 5], and [1] for blow up phenomena.

The doubly parabolic system (PP) has been a bit less studied. For instance, it is known that if for the initial data u0u_{0} one has M<8​πM<8\pi, then positive solutions are global in time, see [12] in the case of a bounded planar domain, and also [3, Theorem 5]. However, it is not known whether M≤8​πM\leq 8\pi is, in general, a necessary condition for the existence of global in time solutions. That is, it is not known whether the blow up occurs for solutions, except for a specific example in [16] of a particular blowing up solution for a system close to (PP). Even, it is an open question what is the exact range of MM guaranteeing the existence of integrable self-similar solutions. For the system (PE) it is proved that M∈[0,8​π)M\in[0,8\pi), and the self-similar solutions (unique for a given M∈[0,8​π)M\in[0,8\pi)) describe the generic asymptotic behaviour of global in time, positive and integrable solutions of (PE). Concerning (PP), it is known that M<M⁡(τ)M<M(\tau) with M⁡(τ)M(\tau) linear in τ\tau, is a necessary condition for the existence of self-similar solutions, cf. [4]. For (PP) with small MM such special solutions are also important in the study of space-time decay of general solutions, see [24]. The analysis if any M>8​πM>8\pi may correspond to a self-similar solution is under way, see [7]. For a different point of view about self-similar solutions for higher dimensional models of (PP), see also [18]. Usual proofs of a blow up for (PE) involve calculations of moments of a solution and then symmetrization, cf. [11, 1]. These methods seem do not work for (PP), hence another approach is needed to show a blow up for that system. For a numerical insight on blow-up issues we refer, e.g., to [14].

A nice result in [25] shows that the solutions of the systems (PP) and (PE) enjoy a kind of stability property as τ↘0\tau\searrow 0: solutions of (PP) converge in a suitable sense to those of (PE). It had been an old question raised by J. J. L. Velázquez and D. Wrzosek, recently solved in [25]. However, this result obtained for suitably small solutions in quite a big functional space of pseudomeasures, gives no indication on the behaviour of possible (“large”) blowing up solutions.

The solvability of the systems (PE), (PP) has been studied in various classes of functions and distributions, like Lebesgue, Morrey, Besov, etc., with an immediate motivation to include the a priori strongest possible critical singularities of either solutions or initial data which appear to be point measures in the two-dimensional case and the multiples of |x|−2|x|^{-2} function in the higher dimensional case. In particular, “vast” functional spaces suitable for analysis of the two-dimensional systems include measure and pseudomeasure spaces, cf. [2, 3, 6, 25].

We show in this paper a result on the existence of (in general, nonintegrable) solutions in a class 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} of functions with natural space-time decay properties, see Theorem 2.1 and 3.1. Here, the space EE of admissible initial conditions also contains Dirac measures. The corresponding solutions may be positive and “large” in the sense of their nonintegrability. Nevertheless, they are defined globally in time. Unlike the paper [25], we work in (x,t)(x,t) space, when [25] has dealt with the Fourier variables ξ\xi, cf. the formulation (36) below. Such results are obtained by an extension and refinement of techniques used in [5] for (PE) in higher dimensions, but neither for (PP), nor in the two-dimensional case of (PE) which often requires a specific treatement. Moreover, the function spaces that we employ here allow us to deal with data that can be more singular than those considered in [5]. The spaces 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} and EE defined in the next section are, in a sense, critical for that analysis, and have been already considered, in slightly different forms, e.g. in the studies of the Navier–Stokes system in [13, 22].

Our main results are contained in Section 4, where we address the problem of the convergence as τ↘0\tau\searrow 0 of solutions uτu^{\tau} of the system (PP) to the corresponding solutions uu of (PE), in the space 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, arising from small data in EE. Mathematically, our stability result is not included in, and does not imply, that of [25]. However, it seems to us that the use of the natural (x,t)(x,t) variables provides a more immediate physical interpretation. Furthermore, our method looks more flexible, and can be used to prove the stability of the system with respect to stronger topologies. For example, we establish also the convergence in the Lt∞​(Lx1)L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}_{x})-norm for data belonging to E∩L1E\cap L^{1}, and in the Lt,x∞L^{\infty}_{t,x}\,-norm for data in E∩L∞E\cap L^{\infty}. Motivated by [19], we will also address this issue in the more general setting of shift invariant spaces of local measures. The main difficulty for obtaining the convergence uτ→uu^{\tau}\to u in strong norms is that ∇φτ\nabla\varphi^{\tau} enjoys some kind of instability as τ→0\tau\to 0, in particular in weighted spaces.

Moreover, we give a nonexistence (blow up) result for solutions of (PP) in ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, d≥1d\geq 1, with the positive Fourier transform of u0^\widehat{u_{0}} in the spirit of [23], see Theorem 5.1. These are complex valued solutions with no straightforward physical/biological interpretation. However, such a result tells us that there is no hope to prove the global existence of solutions to (PP) and similar models for arbitrarily large data relying only on size estimates.

2 The parabolic-elliptic system

In order to study the systems (PE) and (PP) we introduce the Banach space 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} of functions u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and the Banach space EE of tempered distributions u0∈𝒮′​(ℝ2)u_{0}\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) by defining the norms

‖u‖𝒳=ess supt>0,x∈ℝ2​(t+|x|2)​|u⁡(x,t)|,\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}=\hbox{ess\,sup}_{t>0,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\,(t+|x|^{2})\,|u(x,t)|, (1)

and

‖u0‖E=‖et​Δ​u0‖𝒳.\|u_{0}\|_{E}=\|e^{t\Delta}u_{0}\|_{\mathcal{X}}. (2)

Here, et​Δe^{t\Delta} denotes the heat semigroup defined by the Gaussian kernel gtg_{t}, gt​(x)=14​π​t​e−14​t​|x|2g_{t}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi t}e^{-\frac{1}{4t}|x|^{2}}. For example, the Dirac mass u0=δu_{0}=\delta in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} is an element of EE. Notice that, by the definition, EE is continuously embedded into the weak Hardy space ℋw1\mathcal{H}^{1}_{w}, which is the space consisting of all tempered distributions ff such that supt>0|et​Δ​f|\sup_{t>0}|e^{t\Delta}f| belongs to the Lorentz space L1,∞​(ℝ2)L^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}). See [21].

Let us define the bilinear form B0B_{0} by

B0(u,v)(t)≡∫0te(t−s)​Δ∇⋅(u∇(−Δ)−1v)(s)ds.B_{0}(u,v)(t)\equiv\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}v)(s)\,{\rm d}s. (3)

Here, (−Δ)−1(-\Delta)^{-1} is the convolution operator on functions defined on ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} with the kernel K⁡(x)=−12​π​log⁡|x|K(x)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|x|. With this notation, the equivalent integral (mild) formulation to (PE), called also the Duhamel formula, reads

u⁡(t)=et​Δ​u0−B0​(u,u).u(t)=e^{t\Delta}u_{0}-B_{0}(u,u). (4)

We begin by establishing the following simple result

Theorem 2.1

There exist two absolute constants ϵ,β>0\epsilon,\beta>0 with the following property. Let u0∈Eu_{0}\in E be such that ‖u0‖E<ϵ\|u_{0}\|_{E}<\epsilon. Then there exists a unique (mild) solution u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}} of (PE) such that ‖u‖𝒳≤ϵ​β\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq\epsilon\beta.

The proof of Theorem 2.1 will follow from a series of lemmata.

First, we have the following estimate of the leading term in ∇φ\nabla\varphi

Let u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}} and φ\varphi be such that Δ​φ+u=0\Delta\varphi+u=0. Then

∇φ​(x,t)=c0​x|x|2​∫|y|≤|x|/2u⁡(y,t)​𝑑y+ℛ⁡(x,t)\nabla\varphi(x,t)=\frac{c_{0}\,x}{|x|^{2}}\int_{|y|\leq|x|/2}u(y,t)\,{\rm d}y+\mathcal{R}(x,t) (5)

with c0=−12​πc_{0}=-\frac{1}{2\pi} and the remainder ℛ\mathcal{R} satisfying

|ℛ⁡(x,t)|≤C​‖u‖𝒳​(t12+|x|)−1.|\mathcal{R}(x,t)|\leq C\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}+|x|\right)^{-1}.

∂jφ=c0​xj|x|2∗u≡I1+I2+I3,\partial_{j}\varphi=\frac{c_{0}x_{j}}{|x|^{2}}*u\equiv I_{1}+I_{2}+I_{3},

Lemma 2.2

Let u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}} and Δ​φ+u=0\Delta\varphi+u=0. Then

‖∇φ​(t)‖L∞≤C​‖u‖𝒳​t−12.\|\nabla\varphi(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}\,t^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

Lemma 2.3

‖B0​(u,v)‖𝒳≤C0​‖u‖𝒳​‖v‖𝒳.\|B_{0}(u,v)\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq C_{0}\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}\|v\|_{\mathcal{X}}.

But we may represent B0B_{0} as

3 The parabolic-parabolic system

Let τ>0\tau>0 be a fixed parameter. We consider the system (PP) whose equivalent integral formulation reads

u(t)=et​Δu0−∫0t∇⋅e(t−s)​Δ[u(s)1τ∇∫0se1τ​(s−σ)​Δu(σ)dσ]ds.u(t)=e^{t\Delta}u_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\nabla\cdot e^{(t-s)\Delta}\biggl[u(s)\frac{1}{\tau}\nabla\int_{0}^{s}e^{\frac{1}{\tau}(s-\sigma)\Delta}u(\sigma)\,{\rm d}\sigma\biggr]\,{\rm d}s. (16)

We introduce for all τ≥0\tau\geq 0 the bilinear form BτB_{\tau} (recall that GG is defined by the expression (7))

Bτ​(u,v)​(x,t)≡∫0t∫G⁡(x−y,t−s)​(u​Wτ​(v))​(y,s)​𝑑y​𝑑s,B_{\tau}(u,v)(x,t)\equiv\int_{0}^{t}\!\!\int G(x-y,t-s)\bigl(u\,W_{\tau}(v)\bigr)(y,s)\,{\rm d}y\,{\rm d}s, (17)

where Wτ​(v)W_{\tau}(v) is the linear operator acting on vv

Wτ​(v)​(x,t)=∫0t1τ​[G⁡(t−στ)∗v⁡(σ)]​(x,σ)​𝑑σfor​τ>0,W_{\tau}(v)(x,t)=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{\tau}\biggl[G\Bigl(\frac{t-\sigma}{\tau}\Bigr)*v(\sigma)\biggr](x,\sigma)\,{\rm d}\sigma\ \ \ {\rm{for\ }}\tau>0, (18a)
with a natural convention
W0(v)(x,t)=(∇(−Δ)−1v)(x,t).W_{0}(v)(x,t)=\left(\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}v\right)(x,t). (18b)

In this way, the system (PP) is also rewritten in a compact form (cf. (4)) as

u=et​Δ​u0−Bτ​(u,u).u=e^{t\Delta}u_{0}-B_{\tau}(u,u). (19)

We are going to solve (19) in the space 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} exactly as was in the parabolic-elliptic case. An additional estimate, however, is needed:

Lemma 3.1

Let u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}} and τ>0\tau>0. Then there exists a constant C∗>0C^{*}>0, independent of uu and τ\tau, such that

‖Wτ​(u)​(t)‖L∞≤C∗​t−12​‖u‖𝒳.\|W_{\tau}(u)(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq{C^{*}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}. (20)

Proof. As usual we can and do assume ‖u‖𝒳=1\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}=1. Then, for all 1<p≤∞1<p\leq\infty we have

|u⁡(x,σ)|≤|x|−2p​σ−1+1p.|u(x,\sigma)|\leq|x|^{-\frac{2}{p}}\sigma^{-1+\frac{1}{p}}.

This implies, for 1<p≤∞1<p\leq\infty,

‖u⁡(σ)‖Lp,∞≤σ−1+1p.\|u(\sigma)\|_{L^{p,\infty}}\leq\sigma^{-1+\frac{1}{p}}.

Now, we represent

Wτ​(u)=I1+I2,W_{\tau}(u)=I_{1}+I_{2},

where I1=∫0t/2…I_{1}=\int_{0}^{t/2}\dots and I2=∫t/2t…I_{2}=\int_{t/2}^{t}\dots . Evidently, we obtain the bound

‖I1​(t)‖L∞≤C​∫0t/2‖1τ​G​(t−στ)‖L2,1​‖u⁡(σ)‖L2,∞​𝑑σ≤C​t−12.\begin{split}\|I_{1}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}&\leq C\int_{0}^{t/2}\left\|\frac{1}{\tau}G\Bigl(\frac{t-\sigma}{\tau}\Bigr)\right\|_{L^{2,1}}\|u(\sigma)\|_{L^{2,\infty}}\,{\rm d}\sigma\\ &\leq Ct^{-\frac{1}{2}}.\end{split}

For the integral I2I_{2}, let us begin with a rough bound

‖I2​(t)‖L∞≤C​∫t/2t‖1τ​G​(t−στ)‖L1​‖u⁡(σ)‖L∞​𝑑σ≤C​τ−12​t−12.\begin{split}\|I_{2}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}&\leq C\int_{t/2}^{t}\left\|\frac{1}{\tau}G\Bigl(\frac{t-\sigma}{\tau}\Bigr)\right\|_{L^{1}}\|u(\sigma)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,{\rm d}\sigma\\ &\leq C\tau^{-\frac{1}{2}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}.\end{split} (21)

This bound gives the required estimate, excepted when τ\tau belongs to a neighbourhood of the origin. Thus, in the sequel, it is enough to consider the case 0<τ<120<\tau<\frac{1}{2}. Now, we further decompose

I2≡I2,1+I2,2,I_{2}\equiv I_{2,1}+I_{2,2},

where I2,1=∫t/2t−τ​t…I_{2,1}=\int_{t/2}^{t-\tau t}\dots and I2,2=∫t−τ​tt…I_{2,2}=\int_{t-\tau t}^{t}\dots . Next, we are going to improve (21) writing

‖I2,1​(t)‖L∞≤C​∫t/2t−τ​t‖1τ​G​(t−στ)‖L3,1​‖u⁡(σ)‖L32,∞​𝑑σ≤C​τ16​∫t/2t−τ​t(t−σ)−76​σ−13​𝑑σ≤C​t−12.\begin{split}\|I_{2,1}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}&\leq C\int_{t/2}^{t-\tau t}\left\|\frac{1}{\tau}G\Bigl(\frac{t-\sigma}{\tau}\Bigr)\right\|_{L^{3,1}}\|u(\sigma)\|_{L^{\frac{3}{2},\infty}}\,{\rm d}\sigma\\ &\leq C\tau^{\frac{1}{6}}\int_{t/2}^{t-\tau t}(t-\sigma)^{-\frac{7}{6}}\sigma^{-\frac{1}{3}}\,{\rm d}\sigma\\ &\leq Ct^{-\frac{1}{2}}.\end{split} (22)

The last estimate is

‖I2,2​(t)‖L∞≤C​∫t−τ​tt‖1τ​G​(t−στ)‖L1​‖u⁡(σ)‖L∞​𝑑σ≤C​τ−12​∫t−τ​tt(t−σ)−12​σ−1​𝑑σ≤C​t−12.\begin{split}\|I_{2,2}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}&\leq C\int_{t-\tau t}^{t}\left\|\frac{1}{\tau}G\Bigl(\frac{t-\sigma}{\tau}\Bigr)\right\|_{L^{1}}\|u(\sigma)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,{\rm d}\sigma\\ &\leq C\tau^{-\frac{1}{2}}\int_{t-\tau t}^{t}(t-\sigma)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sigma^{-1}\,{\rm d}\sigma\\ &\leq Ct^{-\frac{1}{2}}.\end{split} (23)

The conclusion of Lemma 3.1 follows from (21), (22), (23).          

Lemma 3.1 allows us to see that, if u,v∈𝒳u,\,v\in{\mathcal{X}} with ‖u‖𝒳=‖v‖𝒳=1\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}=\|v\|_{\mathcal{X}}=1, then

|u​Wτ​(v)|​(x,t)≤C​|x|−32​t−34,|u\,W_{\tau}(v)|(x,t)\leq C|x|^{-\frac{3}{2}}t^{-\frac{3}{4}}, (24a)
and
|u​Wτ​(v)|​(x,t)≤C​|x|−2​t−12,|u\,W_{\tau}(v)|(x,t)\leq C|x|^{-2}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}, (24b)
for some constant C>0C>0 independent of τ>0\tau>0.

These are the analogous estimates as those we obtained in the parabolic-elliptic case (see inequalities (6a) and (6b)). Then, using exactly the same arguments as in the previous section, we arrive at the following existence result

Theorem 3.1

There exist two absolute constants ϵ∗,β∗>0\epsilon^{*},\beta^{*}>0 with the following property. Let u0∈Eu_{0}\in E be such that ‖u0‖E<ϵ∗\|u_{0}\|_{E}<\epsilon^{*}. Then there exists a unique (mild) solution u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}} of (PP) such that ‖u‖𝒳≤ϵ∗​β∗\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq\epsilon^{*}\beta^{*}.

Remark. The case of nonzero initial data φ⁡(0)\varphi(0) can be studied in a quite similar way.

Remark. A closer look at the proofs of estimates for ∇φ\nabla\varphi in (PE) and (PP) reveals that the behaviour of ∇φ\nabla\varphi is a bit different in these two cases. Namely, if 0≢u0\not\equiv u and u⁡(x,t)∼(t+|x|2)−1u(x,t)\sim(t+|x|^{2})^{-1} (in the sense that c1​(t+|x|2)−1≤u⁡(x,t)≤c2​(t+|x|2)−1c_{1}(t+|x|^{2})^{-1}\leq u(x,t)\leq c_{2}(t+|x|^{2})^{-1} for some c1,c2>0c_{1},\,c_{2}>0), then it follows from (5) that ∇φ​(x,t)∼|x|−1​log⁡(t+|x|2)\nabla\varphi(x,t)\sim|x|^{-1}\log(t+|x|^{2}) for (PE), while ∇φ\nabla\varphi is more regular: |∇φ​(x,t)|≤c​(t12+|x|)−1|\nabla\varphi(x,t)|\leq c\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}+|x|\right)^{-1} in (PP) case. In other words, letting 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be the space of functions f=f⁡(x,t)f=f(x,t) such that f2∈𝒳f^{2}\in{\mathcal{X}}, we have φτ∈𝒴\varphi^{\tau}\in\mathcal{Y} for τ>0\tau>0, but (φτ)(\varphi^{\tau}) does not converge in 𝒴\mathcal{Y} as τ→0\tau\to 0. However, such an instability does not prevent from the convergence of the densities uτ→uu^{\tau}\to u for vanishing τ\tau.

4 Study of the τ↘0\tau\searrow 0 limit

We now study the convergence as τ↘0\tau\searrow 0 of solutions uτu^{\tau} of the system (PP) to the corresponding solution uu of (PE). A result in this direction has been obtained recently by A. Raczyński in [25], who established the convergence uτ→uu^{\tau}\to u in the norm 𝒴α\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}, for α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2), defined as

‖u‖𝒴α=ess​​supt>0,ξ∈ℝ2(1+t12​|ξ|)α​|u^​(ξ,t)|.\|u\|_{\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}}=\hbox{ess\!}\sup_{\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!t>0,\,\xi\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\left(1+t^{\frac{1}{2}}|\xi|\right)^{\alpha}|\widehat{u}(\xi,t)|. (25)

We will obtain in subsection 4.2 a similar result using the 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}-norm.

4.1 Regularity properties of solutions of (PE)

In this subsection we prepare some preliminary material. The first Proposition consists of a regularity result with respect to the space variable for solutions of (PE). The second Proposition describes their regularity properties with respect to the time variable.

Proposition 4.1

For all r∈(1,2)r\in(1,2) there exists a constant ϵr\epsilon_{r}, with 0<ϵr≤ϵ0<\epsilon_{r}\leq\epsilon (the absolute constant of Theorem 2.1) such that, if ‖u0‖E<ϵr\|u_{0}\|_{E}<\epsilon_{r}, then the solution of (PE) constructed in Theorem 2.1 satisfies

‖∇u​(t)‖Lr,∞≤C​t−32+1r,\displaystyle\left\|\nabla u(t)\right\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}, (26)

for some constant C=C⁡(u0,r)C=C(u_{0},r) independent of tt.

Proof. We use a standard argument involving the subspace 𝒳r⊂𝒳{\mathcal{X}}_{r}\subset{\mathcal{X}} defined by

𝒳r={u∈𝒳,∃C:∥∇u(t)∥Lr,∞≤Ct−32+1r},\displaystyle{\mathcal{X}}_{r}=\Bigl\{u\in{\mathcal{X}},\;\exists\,C\colon\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}\Bigr\},

and equipped with its natural norm. Recalling that the kernel c0​x|x|2\frac{c_{0}x}{|x|^{2}} of the operator ∇(−Δ)−1\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1} belongs to L2,∞L^{2,\infty}, first we deduce from the Young inequality

‖∇2(−Δ)−1​v​(t)‖Lα,∞≤C​t−32+1r​‖v‖𝒳r,1α=1r−12.\displaystyle\left\|\nabla^{2}(-\Delta)^{-1}v(t)\right\|_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}\|v\|_{{\mathcal{X}}_{r}},\qquad\textstyle\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{2}. (27)

Next, from the Hölder inequality (noticing that ‖u⁡(t)‖L2,∞≤C​t−12​‖u‖𝒳\|u(t)\|_{L^{2,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}),

‖u​∇2(−Δ)−1​v​(t)‖Lr,∞≤C​t−2+1r​‖u‖𝒳​‖v‖𝒳r.\displaystyle\|u\nabla^{2}(-\Delta)^{-1}v(t)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-2+\frac{1}{r}}\|u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\|v\|_{{\mathcal{X}}_{r}}. (28)

The generalization of the classical inequalities to Lorentz spaces can be found, e.g., in [19].

We claim that the bilinear operator B0B_{0} introduced in (3) is boundedly defined: B0:𝒳r×𝒳r→𝒳rB_{0}\colon{\mathcal{X}}_{r}\times{\mathcal{X}}_{r}\to{\mathcal{X}}_{r}. Indeed, for ‖u‖𝒳r=‖v‖𝒳r=1\|u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}_{r}}=\|v\|_{{\mathcal{X}}_{r}}=1, we combine the estimates

‖∇G​(t−s)‖1≤C​(t−s)−1\|\nabla G(t-s)\|_{1}\leq C(t-s)^{-1}

and (10) with the inequality (a consequence of u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}})

‖u⁡(s)‖Lr,∞≤C​s−1+1r,\|u(s)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Cs^{-1+\frac{1}{r}}, (29)

the estimate ∥∇(−Δ)−1v(s)∥∞≤Cs−12\|\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}v(s)\|_{\infty}\leq Cs^{-\frac{1}{2}} obtained from Lemma 2.2, and (28). Then we arrive at

‖∇B0​(u,v)​(t)‖Lr,∞\displaystyle\|\nabla B_{0}(u,v)(t)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}
≤C∫0t/2(t−s)−1∥u(s)∥Lr,∞∥∇(−Δ)−1v(s)∥∞ds\displaystyle\qquad\leq C\int_{0}^{t/2}(t-s)^{-1}\|u(s)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\|\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}v(s)\|_{\infty}\,{\rm d}s
+C∫t/2t(t−s)−12(∥∇u(s)∥Lr,∞∥∇(−Δ)−1v(s)∥∞+s−2+1r)ds\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+C\int_{t/2}^{t}(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\Bigl(\|\nabla u(s)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\|\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}v(s)\|_{\infty}+s^{-2+\frac{1}{r}}\Bigr)\,{\rm d}s
≤C​t−32+1r.\displaystyle\qquad\leq Ct^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}.

Moreover, for u0∈Eu_{0}\in E, we have |et2​Δ​u0​(x)|≤C​(t+|x|2)−1|e^{\frac{t}{2}\Delta}u_{0}(x)|\leq C(t+|x|^{2})^{-1}. Hence, ‖et2​Δ​u0‖Lγ,∞≤C​t−1+1γ\|e^{\frac{t}{2}\Delta}u_{0}\|_{L^{\gamma,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-1+\frac{1}{\gamma}} for 1<γ<∞1<\gamma<\infty. We now choose β,γ∈(1,∞)\beta,\gamma\in(1,\infty) such that 1+1r=1β+1γ1+\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}. Then, the semigroup property of the heat kernel gtg_{t}, and the fact that ∇gt/2∈Lβ,1\nabla g_{t/2}\in L^{\beta,1}, imply

∥∇et​Δu0∥Lr,∞≤Ct−32+1r.\displaystyle\|\nabla e^{t\Delta}u_{0}\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}.

Now the usual the application of the contraction mapping theorem, in a closed ball of small radius in the space 𝒳r{\mathcal{X}}_{r}, allows us to conclude.          

The following proposition is the first crucial tool for our stability result. It provides the Hölder regularity, with respect to the time variable, of solutions of (PE) in Lorentz spaces.

Proposition 4.2

Let 1<r<21<r<2 and u0∈Eu_{0}\in E, such that ‖u0‖E<ϵr\|u_{0}\|_{E}<\epsilon_{r}. Then the solution uu of (PE) constructed in Proposition 4.1 satisfies for all 0<t′<t0<t^{\prime}<t

‖u⁡(t)−u⁡(t′)‖Lr,∞≤C​(t−t′)12​(t′)−32+1r,\|u(t)-u(t^{\prime})\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq C(t-t^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{2}}(t^{\prime})^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}, (30)

et​Δ​u0​(x)−et′​Δ​u0​(x)=∫(et′​Δ​u0​(x−y)−et′​Δ​u0​(x))​gt−t′​(y)​𝑑y=−∫∫01∇et′​Δu0(x−θy)⋅ygt−t′(y)dydθ,\begin{split}e^{t\Delta}u_{0}(x)-e^{t^{\prime}\Delta}u_{0}(x)&=\int\Bigl(e^{t^{\prime}\Delta}u_{0}(x-y)-e^{t^{\prime}\Delta}u_{0}(x)\Bigr)g_{t-t^{\prime}}(y)\,{\rm d}y\\ &=-\int\!\!\int_{0}^{1}\nabla e^{t^{\prime}\Delta}u_{0}(x-\theta y)\cdot yg_{t-t^{\prime}}(y)\,{\rm d}y\,{\rm d}\theta,\end{split}

‖et​Δ​u0−et′​Δ​u0‖Lr,∞≤C∥∇et′​Δu0∥Lr,∞∥ygt−t′∥1≤C​(t−t′)12​(t′)−32+1r.\begin{split}\|e^{t\Delta}u_{0}-e^{t^{\prime}\Delta}u_{0}\|_{L^{r,\infty}}&\leq C\|\nabla e^{t^{\prime}\Delta}u_{0}\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\|yg_{t-t^{\prime}}\|_{1}\\ &\leq C(t-t^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{2}}(t^{\prime})^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}.\end{split}

Now, we can write

B0​(u,u)​(t)−B0​(u,u)​(t′)=A1+A2,B_{0}(u,u)(t)-B_{0}(u,u)(t^{\prime})=A_{1}+A_{2},

and

Recall that from u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}} we deduce (29). Combining this with the estimate of Lemma 2.2 we get

‖u∇(−Δ)−1u(s)‖Lr,∞≤Cs−32+1r.\left\|u\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}u(s)\right\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Cs^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}. (31)

This immediately yields

‖A2‖Lr,∞≤∫t′t(t−s)−12​s−32+1r​ds≤C​(t−t′)12​(t′)−32+1r.\begin{split}\|A_{2}\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}}s^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}\,{\rm d}s\leq C(t-t^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigl(t^{\prime}\bigr)^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}}.\end{split}

The estimate of A1A_{1} is slightly more involved. We start with the identity

G⁡(t−s)−G⁡(t′−s)=(e(t−t′)​Δ−Id)​G​(t′−s).G(t-s)-G(t^{\prime}-s)=\left(e^{(t-t^{\prime})\Delta}-{\rm Id}\right)G(t^{\prime}-s).

The action of the convolution operator with the function on the right hand side is studied via the following variant of a result established in [20].

Lemma 4.1

Denote the Calderón operator by Λ=(−Δ)12\Lambda=(-\Delta)^{\frac{1}{2}}. Then, for some constant CC depending only on r∈(1,∞)r\in(1,\infty)

‖(et​Δ−Id)​f‖Lr,∞≤C​t12​‖Λ​f‖Lr,∞.\bigl\|\bigl(e^{t\Delta}-{\rm Id}\bigr)f\bigr\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Ct^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\Lambda f\|_{L^{r,\infty}}.

Proof. Writing f=Λ−1​Λ​ff=\Lambda^{-1}\Lambda f, we see that

(et​Δ−Id)​f=Φt∗(Λ​f),\bigl(e^{t\Delta}-{\rm Id}\bigr)f=\Phi_{t}*(\Lambda f),

where,

Φ^t​(ξ)=t12​Φ^​(t12​ξ),\widehat{\Phi}_{t}(\xi)=t^{\frac{1}{2}}\widehat{\Phi}(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\xi),

and

Φ^​(ξ)=(e−|ξ|2−1)​|ξ|−1.\widehat{\Phi}(\xi)=(e^{-|\xi|^{2}}-1)|\xi|^{-1}.

Φ(x)=−2∫1∞Ψ(ηx)dη.\Phi(x)=-2\int_{1}^{\infty}\Psi(\eta\,x)\,{\rm d}\eta.
 

    

 

Using this Lemma we deduce

‖A1‖Lr,∞≤C(t−t′)12∫0t′∥Λ∇gt′−s∗(u∇(−Δ)−1u)(s)∥Lr,∞ds=C​(t−t′)12​(A1,1+A1,2),\begin{split}\|A_{1}\|_{L^{r,\infty}}&\leq C(t-t^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{2}}\int_{0}^{t^{\prime}}\|\Lambda\nabla g_{t^{\prime}-s}*\left(u\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}u\right)(s)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\,{\rm d}s\\ &=C(t-t^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{2}}(A_{1,1}+A_{1,2}),\end{split}

4.2 The vanishing τ\tau limit

After Proposition 4.2, the second crucial step for the study of the limit as τ↘0\tau\searrow 0 consists in the asymptotic analysis of the linear operators WτW_{\tau}, τ≥0\tau\geq 0, introduced in (18a)–(18b). This is the purpose of the following lemma.

Lemma 4.2

Let ε=ε⁡(τ)\varepsilon=\varepsilon(\tau) be an arbitrary function, strictly increasing and continuous on [0,1][0,1], such that ε⁡(0)=0\varepsilon(0)=0. Let also 1<r<21<r<2 and uu be a function satisfying, for 0<t′<t0<t^{\prime}<t,

‖u⁡(t)‖Lr,∞≤C​t−1+1r,‖u⁡(t)−u⁡(t′)‖Lr,∞≤C​(t−t′)12​(t′)−32+1r,\begin{split}&\|u(t)\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq Ct^{-1+\frac{1}{r}},\\ &\|u(t)-u(t^{\prime})\|_{L^{r,\infty}}\leq C(t-t^{\prime})^{\frac{1}{2}}(t^{\prime})^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{r}},\end{split} (32)

with a constant CC independent of t,t′t,t^{\prime}. Then, for all t>0t>0, τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], and for another constant CC, independent of tt and τ\tau,

ε⁡(τ)​supt>0t12​‖(Wτ​(u)−W0​(u))​(t)‖∞≤C​τ1r−12.\varepsilon(\tau)\sup_{t>0}t^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\|\left(W_{\tau}(u)-W_{0}(u)\right)(t)\right\|_{\infty}\leq C\tau^{\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{2}}. (33)

In particular, if u0∈Eu_{0}\in E is small enough (for example, ‖u0‖E≤ϵ3/2\|u_{0}\|_{E}\leq\epsilon_{3/2}), then the corresponding solution uu of (PE) constructed in Proposition 4.1 satisfies

limτ→0supt>0t12​‖(Wτ​(u)−W0​(u))​(t)‖∞=0.\lim_{\tau\to 0}\,\,\sup_{t>0}t^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\|\left(W_{\tau}(u)-W_{0}(u)\right)(t)\right\|_{\infty}=0. (34)

Proof. Without any restriction we can assume that 0<ε⁡(τ)<120<\varepsilon(\tau)<\frac{1}{2} for positive τ\tau. Define ε~​(τ)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau) such that ε=ε~1r−12\varepsilon=\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{2}}. Borrowing from [25] the idea of splitting the time integral using intervals depending on τ\tau, we write

Wτ​(u)−W0​(u)≡J1+J2+J3,W_{\tau}(u)-W_{0}(u)\equiv J_{1}+J_{2}+J_{3},

where

J1​(t)=∫0t​(1−ε~​(τ))[1τ​G​(t−sτ)∗u⁡(s)]​𝑑s,J_{1}(t)=\int_{0}^{t(1-\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau))}\biggl[\frac{1}{\tau}G\Bigl(\frac{t-s}{\tau}\Bigr)*u(s)\biggr]\,{\rm d}s,

next

J2​(t)=∫t​(1−ε~​(τ))t1τ​G​(t−sτ)∗u⁡(t)​𝑑s−W0​(u)​(t),J_{2}(t)=\int_{t(1-\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau))}^{t}\frac{1}{\tau}G\Bigl(\frac{t-s}{\tau}\Bigr)*u(t)\,{\rm d}s\;-\;W_{0}(u)(t),

and

J3​(t)=∫t​(1−ε~​(τ))t1τ​G​(t−sτ)∗[u⁡(s)−u⁡(t)]​𝑑s.J_{3}(t)=\int_{t(1-\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau))}^{t}\frac{1}{\tau}G\Bigl(\frac{t-s}{\tau}\Bigr)*\bigl[u(s)-u(t)\bigr]\,{\rm d}s.

From the first relation of (32) and the Young inequality in Lorentz space (using that, by (7), G⁡(⋅,t)∈Lr′,1​(ℝ2)G(\cdot,t)\in L^{r^{\prime},1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), where r′r^{\prime} is the conjugate exponent), we get

‖J1​(t)‖∞≤C​τ1r−12​∫0t​(1−ε~​(τ))(t−s)−12−1r​s−1+1r​𝑑s≤C​(τε~​(τ))1r−12​t−12.\begin{split}\|J_{1}(t)\|_{\infty}&\leq C\tau^{\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{2}}\int_{0}^{t(1-\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau))}(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{r}}s^{-1+\frac{1}{r}}\,{\rm d}s\\ &\leq C\left(\frac{\tau}{\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau)}\right)^{\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{2}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}.\end{split}

Notice that this estimate of J1J_{1} is exactly what we need for (33).

As for J2J_{2}, we see from a simple computation via the Fourier transform that

J2(t)=−gt​ε~​(τ)/τ∗W0(u)(t).J_{2}(t)=-g_{t\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau)/\tau}*W_{0}(u)(t).

Applying once more the Young inequality (using now gt​ε~​(τ)/τ∈Lα′,1g_{t\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau)/\tau}\in L^{\alpha^{\prime},1}), we get, as before,

‖J2​(t)‖∞≤C​(τε~​(τ))1r−12​t−12.\|J_{2}(t)\|_{\infty}\leq C\left(\frac{\tau}{\tilde{\varepsilon}(\tau)}\right)^{\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{2}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

which is even better than what we need. This proves the inequality (33). Choosing, for example, r=32r=\frac{3}{2} and ε⁡(τ)=12​τ1/12\varepsilon(\tau)=\frac{1}{2}\tau^{1/12} proves the last claim (34) of Lemma 4.2.          

We are now in the position of establishing our first main result

Theorem 4.1

There exists an absolute constant ϵ′>0\epsilon^{\prime}>0 (a priori smaller than the constants ϵ,ϵ∗>0\epsilon,\epsilon^{*}>0 in Theorems 2.1 and 3.1), such that if u0∈Eu_{0}\in E, ‖u0‖E<ϵ′\|u_{0}\|_{E}<\epsilon^{\prime}, then denoting by u∈𝒳u\in{\mathcal{X}} the solution of (PE) and uτ∈𝒳u^{\tau}\in{\mathcal{X}} the solution of (PP) constructed in the previous theorems, we have as τ↘0\tau\searrow 0

uτ→uin 𝒳.u^{\tau}\to u\qquad\hbox{in\ \ ${\mathcal{X}}$}.

Proof. The proof follows easily from Lemma 4.2. Indeed, from the integral equations (4) and (19), the bilinearity of BτB_{\tau} and B0B_{0}, and the smallness of the solutions uτu^{\tau} and uu, we have (similarly as in [25], where two terms in the bilinear expansion can be absorbed by the left hand side)

‖uτ−u‖𝒳≤C​‖Bτ​(u,u)−B0​(u,u)‖𝒳.\|u^{\tau}-u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\leq C\|B_{\tau}(u,u)-B_{0}(u,u)\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}.

But, by the definition of WτW_{\tau} and W0W_{0} (see (18a)-(18b)),

Bτ​(u,u)​(t)−B0​(u,u)​(t)=∫0tG⁡(t−s)∗(u⁡(Wτ​(u)−W0​(u)))​(s)​𝑑s.B_{\tau}(u,u)(t)-B_{0}(u,u)(t)=\int_{0}^{t}G(t-s)*\bigl(u(W_{\tau}(u)-W_{0}(u))\bigr)(s)\,ds.

Argueing as in the proof of Lemma 2.3, we obtain

‖Bτ​(u,u)−B0​(u,u)‖𝒳≤C​‖u‖𝒳​(supt>0t12​‖Wτ​(u)−W0​(u)​(t)‖∞).\|B_{\tau}(u,u)-B_{0}(u,u)\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\leq C\|u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\Bigl(\sup_{t>0}{t^{\frac{1}{2}}}\|W_{\tau}(u)-W_{0}(u)(t)\|_{\infty}\Bigr).

If ϵ′>0\epsilon^{\prime}>0 is small enough, then Lemma 4.2 can be applied to the solution uu of (PE), implying that the right hand side of the above inequality has a vanishing limit for small τ\tau. This finally gives

‖uτ−u‖𝒳→0as τ↘0.\|u^{\tau}-u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\to 0\qquad\hbox{as \ \ $\tau\searrow 0$}.
 

    

 
Remark 4.1

Notice that, the smaller the norm ‖u0‖E\|u_{0}\|_{E}, the faster the convergence uτ→uu^{\tau}\to u as τ→0\tau\to 0. This is due to the fact that for very small data it is possible to apply Lemma 4.2 with rr close to 11 (despite the constants in our estimates blow up as r↘1r\searrow 1). More precisely, our arguments show that for any 0<δ<120<\delta<\frac{1}{2}, one can find a constant C>0C>0 and ϵ⁡(δ)>0\epsilon(\delta)>0 such that, for ‖u0‖E≤ϵ⁡(δ)\|u_{0}\|_{E}\leq\epsilon(\delta), one has ‖uτ−u‖𝒳≤C​τ12−δ\|u^{\tau}-u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\leq C\tau^{\frac{1}{2}-\delta} for all 0≤τ≤10\leq\tau\leq 1.

4.3 The parabolic-elliptic limit in stronger topologies

If u0≥0u_{0}\geq 0 is small in the EE-norm, and belongs to a smaller space, for example, u0∈E∩L1u_{0}\in E\cap L^{1}, then the solutions uτu^{\tau} and uu of (PP) and (PE) will remain in L1L^{1}, uniformly in time, during their evolution. Hence, it is natural to ask whether the convergence uτ→uu^{\tau}\to u holds also in the natural norm of L∞​((0,∞),L1)L^{\infty}((0,\infty);L^{1}). Our next theorem provides a positive answer. As the proof of this fact does not really depend on a particular topology under consideration, it seems appropriate to consider a more abstract setting.

We denote by ℒ\mathcal{L} any shift invariant Banach space of local measures, see [19, Ch. 4] for their definition and main properties. These are Banach spaces of distributions, continuously embedded in 𝒟′​(ℝ2)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}). Moreover, they are known to satisfy the following properties (for some constant C>0C>0 depending only on ℒ\mathcal{L}),

  1. 1.

    For all f∈ℒ,g∈L1​(ℝ2)f\in\mathcal{L},\;g\in L^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), the convolution product f∗gf*g is well defined in ℒ\mathcal{L} and ‖f∗g‖ℒ≤C​‖f‖ℒ​‖g‖1\|f*g\|_{\mathcal{L}}\leq C\|f\|_{\mathcal{L}}\|g\|_{1}.

  2. 2.

    For all f∈ℒ,h∈L∞​(ℝ2)f\in\mathcal{L},\;h\in L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), the pointwise product f​hfh is well defined in ℒ\mathcal{L} and ‖f​h‖ℒ≤C​‖f‖ℒ​‖h‖∞\|fh\|_{\mathcal{L}}\leq C\|f\|_{\mathcal{L}}\|h\|_{\infty}.

  3. 3.

    Each bounded sequence {fk}⊂ℒ\{f_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{L} has a subsequence convergent in ℒ\mathcal{L}, in the distributional sense.

Obvious examples of spaces satisfying these properties (and which are indeed shift invariant space of local measures) are the LpL^{p}-spaces, 1<p≤∞1<p\leq\infty, the Lorentz spaces Lp,qL^{p,q}, 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, 1<q≤∞1<q\leq\infty and the space of bounded Borel measures M⁡(ℝ2)=𝒞0​(ℝ2)∗M({\mathbb{R}}^{2})=\mathcal{C}_{0}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})^{*}. In the latter case, such duality relations ensures Property 3. Other interesting examples include the Morrey–Campanato spaces Mp,qM^{p,q}, (1<p≤q<∞1<p\leq q<\infty) and suitable multiplier spaces, see [19, Ch. 17].

On the other hand, the space of pseudomeasures, i.e., the space of tempered distributions ff such that f^∈L∞\widehat{f}\in L^{\infty}) does not fulfill the second requirement. Therefore, the stability result in the pseudomeasure topology will not be encompassed by our next Theorem, but requires a specific (and more involved) treatment, see [25].

Notice that, because of the conservation of the total mass for positive solutions of (PE) and (PP), the L1L^{1}-norm remains constant during the evolution. This observation will allow us to handle the case of data u0∈E∩L1u_{0}\in E\cap L^{1}, despite Property 3 breaks down for L1L^{1}.

Theorem 4.2

Let u0∈E∩ℒu_{0}\in E\cap\mathcal{L}, where ℒ\mathcal{L} is either a shift invariant Banach space of local measures, or ℒ=L1\mathcal{L}=L^{1}. In the latter case we require either u0≥0u_{0}\geq 0 or, for signed u0u_{0}, that ‖u0‖1\|u_{0}\|_{1} is sufficiently small. Then there exists a positive constant ϵ~\tilde{\epsilon} , depending only on ℒ\mathcal{L}, such that, if

‖u0‖E<ϵ~,\|u_{0}\|_{E}<\tilde{\epsilon},

then the systems (PE) and (PP) possess unique solutions uu and uτu^{\tau}, respectively, such that for an absolute constant β~>0\tilde{\beta}>0, ‖u‖𝒳≤β~​ϵ~\|u\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\leq\tilde{\beta}\tilde{\epsilon} and ‖uτ‖𝒳≤β~​ϵ~\|u^{\tau}\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}\leq\tilde{\beta}\tilde{\epsilon}. In addition,

supt>0‖u⁡(t)‖ℒ<∞andsupt>0‖uτ​(t)‖ℒ<∞.\sup_{t>0}\|u(t)\|_{\mathcal{L}}<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sup_{t>0}\|u^{\tau}(t)\|_{\mathcal{L}}<\infty.

Moreover, the conclusion ‖uτ​(t)−u⁡(t)‖𝒳→0\|u^{\tau}(t)-u(t)\|_{\mathcal{X}}\to 0 of Theorem 4.1 is strengthened

supt>0‖uτ​(t)−u⁡(t)‖ℒ→0as τ↘0.\sup_{t>0}\|u^{\tau}(t)-u(t)\|_{\mathcal{L}}\,\to 0\qquad\hbox{as \ $\tau\searrow 0$}.

Proof. Obviously we have, for some constant C0>0C_{0}>0 independent of tt

‖et​Δ​u0‖ℒ≤C0.\|e^{t\Delta}u_{0}\|_{\mathcal{L}}\leq C_{0}.

Moreover, for each τ≥0\tau\geq 0 (we include in this way the analysis of (PE)), we have the estimate

‖Bτ​(u,v)​(t)‖ℒ≤C~​(supt>0‖u⁡(t)‖ℒ)​‖v‖𝒳,\|B_{\tau}(u,v)(t)\|_{\mathcal{L}}\leq\tilde{C}\Bigl(\sup_{t>0}\|u(t)\|_{\mathcal{L}}\Bigr)\|v\|_{{\mathcal{X}}}, (35)

The last factor is bounded by ‖v‖𝒳\|v\|_{{\mathcal{X}}} owing to Lemma 2.2 in the case τ=0\tau=0, and to Lemma 2.3 for τ>0\tau>0. This yields (35).

On the other hand, applying recursively (35), we get ukτ​(t)∈ℒu^{\tau}_{k}(t)\in\mathcal{L} for all kk and

supt>0‖ukτ​(y)‖ℒ≤C0+β~​C~​ϵ~​(supt>0‖uk−1τ​(y)‖ℒ),\sup_{t>0}\|u^{\tau}_{k}(y)\|_{\mathcal{L}}\leq C_{0}+\tilde{\beta}\tilde{C}\tilde{\epsilon}\Bigl(\sup_{t>0}\|u^{\tau}_{k-1}(y)\|_{\mathcal{L}}\Bigr),

as τ↘0\tau\searrow 0, uniformly in (x,t)∈ℝ2×[0,∞)(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times[0,\infty).

5 Blow up of complex valued solutions of the parabolic-parabolic system

Consider the system (PP) in the space ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} with any d≥1d\geq 1. Passing to the Fourier transforms, we may write the Duhamel formula (16) in the form

u^​(ξ,t)=e−t​|ξ|2​u^0​(ξ)+∫0t∫0s∫ℝdξ⋅ητe−(t−s)​|ξ|2e−1τ​(s−σ)​|η|2u^(ξ−η,s)u^(η,σ)dηdσds.\begin{split}&\widehat{u}(\xi,t)=e^{-t|\xi|^{2}}\widehat{u}_{0}(\xi)\\ &\qquad\qquad+\int_{0}^{t}\!\!\int_{0}^{s}\!\!\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\frac{\xi\cdot\eta}{\tau}e^{-(t-s)|\xi|^{2}}e^{-\frac{1}{\tau}(s-\sigma)|\eta|^{2}}\widehat{u}(\xi-\eta,s)\widehat{u}(\eta,\sigma)\,{\rm d}\eta\,{\rm d}\sigma\,{\rm d}s.\end{split} (36)

Our goal is to construct a class of complex valued initial data, such that the corresponding solutions blow up in finite time, in any classical norm. For a∈ℝa\in{\mathbb{R}}, we denote by B˙∞a,∞\dot{B}^{a,\infty}_{\infty} the homogeneous Besov space, which can also be identified with the Hölder–Zygmund space 𝒞˙a\dot{\mathcal{C}}^{a}. As it is well known (see [19, 23]), most of the classical functional spaces (including all homogeneous Triebel–Lizorkin, and thus Lebesgue or Sobolev spaces) are continuously embedded in B˙∞a,∞\dot{B}^{a,\infty}_{\infty} for some real aa.

Theorem 5.1

There exists w0∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)w_{0}\in{\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{R}}^{d}) such that w^0​(ξ)≥0\widehat{w}_{0}(\xi)\geq 0, ‖w^0‖L1=1\|\widehat{w}_{0}\|_{L^{1}}=1. If AA is sufficiently large, then any (tempered) distributional solution of (36) with u0=A​w0u_{0}=Aw_{0} (and thus any solution of (PP)) blows up in a finite time. More precisely, for some time t∗<∞t^{*}<\infty and each a∈ℝa\in{\mathbb{R}}, ‖u⁡(t∗)‖B˙∞a,∞=∞\|u(t^{*})\|_{\dot{B}^{a,\infty}_{\infty}}=\infty holds.

Our approach is closely related to that in [5, Theorem 3.1] which followed the argument in [23] for the “cheap” Navier–Stokes equations. We produce some estimates from below of the Fourier transform of any solution with u⁡(0)=u0u(0)=u_{0} that can be obtained via the iteration procedure for (36) with

uk+1=et​Δu0−∫0t∇⋅e(t−s)​Δ1τ[uk(s)∇∫0se1τ​(s−σ)​Δuk(σ)dσ]ds,u_{k+1}=e^{t\Delta}u_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\nabla\cdot e^{(t-s)\Delta}\frac{1}{\tau}\biggl[u_{k}(s)\nabla\int_{0}^{s}e^{\frac{1}{\tau}(s-\sigma)\Delta}u_{k}(\sigma)\,{\rm d}\sigma\biggr]\,{\rm d}s,

u^​(ξ,t)≥(3​δ​τ−1+e−4​δ​τ)​2−2​k−3​τ−1​e−δ​βk−12​e−2k​t​w^k​(ξ).\begin{split}\widehat{u}(\xi,t)&\geq(3\delta\tau-1+e^{-4\delta\tau})2^{-2k-3}\tau^{-1}e^{-\delta}\beta_{k-1}^{2}e^{-2^{k}\,t}\widehat{w}_{k}(\xi).\\ \end{split}

This inequality is interesting only if the right hand side is positive. Therefore we will assume that 3​δ​τ≥13\delta\tau\geq 1. We choose {βk}\{\beta_{k}\} in such a way that

β0=A,βk=(3δτ−1+e−4​δ​τ)2−2​k−3τ−1e−δβk−12,k=1,2,….\beta_{0}=A,\qquad\beta_{k}=(3\delta\tau-1+e^{-4\delta\tau})2^{-2k-3}\tau^{-1}e^{-\delta}\beta_{k-1}^{2},\qquad k=1,2,\ldots\ .

This choice leads to inequality (37).

In order to compute βk\beta_{k}, we introduce Mδ,τM_{\delta,\tau}, such that

Notice that we have βk=2Mδ,τ−2​k​βk−12\beta_{k}=2^{M_{\delta,\tau}-2k}\beta_{k-1}^{2}. We claim that, for some a,b,c∈ℝa,b,c\in{\mathbb{R}},

Hence, we have

βk=(A 2Mδ,τ−4)2k 24−Mδ,τ+2​k,k=0,1,….\beta_{k}=\Bigl(A\,2^{M_{\delta,\tau}-4}\Bigr)^{2^{k}}\,2^{4-M_{\delta,\tau}+2k},\qquad k=0,1,\ldots\ . (39)

we have by (39) βk→∞\beta_{k}\to\infty and, in particular, ‖u⁡(tk)‖L1=‖u^​(tk)‖∞→∞\|u(t_{k})\|_{L^{1}}=\|\widehat{u}(t_{k})\|_{\infty}\to\infty for k→∞k\to\infty. The above size condition on AA can be rewritten in an equivalent form as

(3​δ​τ−1+e−4​δ​τ)​A≥27​eδ​τ.(3\delta\tau-1+e^{-4\delta\tau})A\geq 2^{7}e^{\delta}\,\tau.

A further analysis of the lower bounds obtained for the Fourier transform of a candidate solution permits us to conclude, as was in [5], that ‖u⁡(t∗)‖B˙∞a,∞=∞\|u(t^{*})\|_{\dot{B}^{a,\infty}_{\infty}}=\infty for each a∈ℝa\in{\mathbb{R}}, so that all Besov (and also LpL^{p} or Triebel–Lizorkin) norms of uu blow up not later than t∗t^{*}.
